explanations.explanation: David says his prayer comes from “…lips free of deceit.” (Psalm 17:1) No spin, no sales pitch, no fancy wrapping paper. He's telling it to the LORD straight, and I like that.

I get why this one tempts you, since David has enemies on his mind. But in verse 1 he doesn't mention fear at all. He says his prayer comes from “…lips free of deceit.” (Psalm 17:1) He's talking about how honest his words are.
Quiet doesn't quite fit, friend, because David says, “listen to my cry.” (Psalm 17:1) A cry is not a whisper. He also says the prayer comes from “…lips free of deceit.” (Psalm 17:1)

David says, “You have tested me and found no evil…” (Psalm 17:3) He's saying the LORD tried his heart and even visited him in the night. I think David is laying his whole heart out where God can see it.
Pride is a sneaky one, but David never says that's what God found. He says, “You have tested me and found no evil…” (Psalm 17:3) That's the result he names after the testing and the night visit.
David talks about a tested heart, but he doesn't say God found doubt there. What he says is, “You have tested me and found no evil…” (Psalm 17:3) That's the report David gives.
Yes, David says, “I have resolved not to sin with my mouth.” (Psalm 17:3) He made up his mind about his mouth. Honestly, my mouth could use a resolution like that on a day when I'm hungry.
The text says the opposite, friend. David says, “I have resolved not to sin with my mouth.” (Psalm 17:3) He made up his mind about what comes out of his mouth, so this one is true.
Not quite. David says the very opposite: “My steps have held to Your paths; my feet have not slipped.” (Psalm 17:5) So it's false. His feet stayed on God's paths.

Right, because David says, “My steps have held to Your paths; my feet have not slipped.” (Psalm 17:5) Feet that didn't slip, steps that held. That's a man walking steady, and he's not tiptoeing like the floor is wet.
That's it. David says, “I call on You, O God, for You will answer me.” (Psalm 17:6) He isn't hoping the line picks up. He's sure God will answer him.

Forgiveness is a big and wonderful thing, friend, but it showed up at the wrong verse. David says, “I call on You, O God, for You will answer me.” (Psalm 17:6) Forgive is a fine word, it just didn't get the job here. The word he uses is answer.
Healing is a good guess, but David doesn't say it here. He says, “I call on You, O God, for You will answer me.” (Psalm 17:6) His confidence is that God will answer.

explanations.answer: Those who seek refuge from their foes
explanations.explanation: David says God saves by His right hand “…those who seek refuge from their foes.” (Psalm 17:7) The people he names are the ones who seek refuge. The trouble they're seeking refuge from is their foes.

explanations.answer: Those who are strong enough on their own
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what David says. God saves by His right hand “…those who seek refuge from their foes.” (Psalm 17:7) These are people who run to Him for shelter, not people who handle everything alone.

explanations.answer: Those who bring the biggest offerings
explanations.explanation: Offerings never come up in this verse, friend. David doesn't ask who has the fattest offering. He asks God to save by His right hand “…those who seek refuge from their foes.” (Psalm 17:7) I think that's good news for anybody showing up with empty hands, because the only thing this verse asks you to bring is yourself, running for cover.
David asks to be hidden “…from the wicked who assail me, from my mortal enemies who surround me.” (Psalm 17:8-9) Those are the ones he names. He's asking for shelter from their attack.

Priests? I looked through this whole prayer, friend, and there's not one in it. David asks to be hidden “…from the wicked who assail me, from my mortal enemies who surround me.” (Psalm 17:8-9) Those are the ones he names.

Crowds didn't make the guest list in this prayer, friend. David asks to be hidden “…from the wicked who assail me, from my mortal enemies who surround me.” (Psalm 17:8-9) The ones he names are the wicked and the mortal enemies.
Close, but the text says the opposite. David says, “They have closed their callous hearts; their mouths speak with arrogance.” (Psalm 17:10) Arrogance, not humility. So the answer is false.
That's right. David says, “They have closed their callous hearts; their mouths speak with arrogance.” (Psalm 17:10) Arrogance is what comes out of those mouths. Humility isn't in that picture at all.
Yes, David says, “They have tracked us down, and now surround us…” (Psalm 17:11) They found him, and now they're all around him. That's why he's asking God for shelter.
If only, friend. Ignoring would be a nice, quiet kind of problem. David says, “They have tracked us down, and now surround us…” (Psalm 17:11) They're all around him.
The text doesn't say they fear anyone. It says, “They have tracked us down, and now surround us…” (Psalm 17:11) The word is surround. They're the ones doing the closing in.

David compares them to “…a lion greedy for prey, like a young lion lurking in ambush.” (Psalm 17:12) Both pictures are lions, one hungry and one waiting in hiding. That tells you how David sees the danger around him.

explanations.answer: A bear robbed of her cubs
explanations.explanation: No bear in this psalm, friend. David says his enemies are “…like a lion greedy for prey, like a young lion lurking in ambush.” (Psalm 17:12) He pictures a lion, and that's the animal he picks.

A wolf makes a fine villain, but it's not the one David picks. He says, “…like a lion greedy for prey, like a young lion lurking in ambush.” (Psalm 17:12) The animal is a lion, and he says it twice, a lion and then a young lion.
David prays, “Arise, O LORD, confront them! Bring them to their knees…” (Psalm 17:13) He asks the LORD Himself to step in. David isn't handing this one to anybody else.

explanations.answer: Lead them to make peace with him
explanations.explanation: I love the optimism, friend, but nobody in this verse is scheduling a sit-down over coffee. David prays, “Arise, O LORD, confront them! Bring them to their knees…” (Psalm 17:13) He's not asking for a handshake. He's asking God to step in and stop them. I think when David has run out of his own options, handing it to the LORD is the move.

explanations.answer: Send them away to another land
explanations.explanation: Moving day isn't what David asks for. He prays, “Arise, O LORD, confront them! Bring them to their knees…” (Psalm 17:13) He asks God to confront them and bring them down.
Yes, he says, “May You fill the bellies of Your treasured ones…” (Psalm 17:14) David prays for God's treasured ones to be filled. A full belly is a good thing to ask the LORD for.
The text says he does ask. David prays, “May You fill the bellies of Your treasured ones…” (Psalm 17:14) So the answer is true. He's praying for God's treasured ones to be filled.

David prays that the treasured ones and their sons are satisfied, “…so they leave their abundance to their children.” (Psalm 17:14) The prayer reaches past one generation. He's asking for plenty to be passed down.

Battles is a tempting guess with that lion in the psalm, but David doesn't pray for them to be left behind. He says, “…so they leave their abundance to their children.” (Psalm 17:14) What's handed down is abundance.

That's a heavy thing to hand down, and David doesn't ask for it. His prayer is that they be satisfied, “…so they leave their abundance to their children.” (Psalm 17:14) The thing left behind is abundance.

That's the word. David says, “when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.” (Psalm 17:15) After all the lions and the surrounding and the crying out, his prayer closes on being satisfied in God's presence.
After a psalm full of enemies, I understand the guess. But David ends it differently: “when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.” (Psalm 17:15) The word is satisfied.
Silent isn't the word David uses, friend. He says, “when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.” (Psalm 17:15) He ends on satisfied.
